name: Guardian PocketShock PSR-1 'Nudge'
description:
The Guardian PSR-1 is a micro stun rod approximately the size and weight of a thick marker pen — 14 centimeters long, 1.8 centimeters in diameter, weighing 45 grams. One end is a pocket clip and recessed charge indicator; the other is a blunt contact tip with a single annular electrode. Inside is a single-use compressed capacitor assembly that stores enough energy for three full discharges at 35,000 volts before the capacitor is depleted, at which point the unit is discarded. There is no recharge port — the PSR-1 is a disposable product, sold in two-packs and four-packs at Tier 2 convenience outlets, pharmacies, and transit hub vending machines.

Guardian designed the PSR-1 around the concept of last-resort personal defense — a device so small and so simple that it offers a meaningful option to people who would carry nothing else. The activation mechanism is a deliberate squeeze-and-twist: the user grips the device firmly and rotates the upper third 90 degrees, which both arms the discharge and moves the contact tip to the active position. This prevents pocket activation while remaining operable under stress with one hand. The three-discharge limit is not a compromise — Guardian's research indicated that most defensive incidents requiring a shock weapon require one to two discharges, and a three-discharge limit keeps the capacitor assembly small enough for the form factor.

The PSR-1 is the most widely sold shock device in GLMZ by unit volume. Its Φ28 two-pack price point makes it accessible to Tier 1 residents in a way that no licensed security product is. Guardian's marketing for the PSR-1 is deliberately quiet — no dramatic imagery, no explicit weapon framing, just the phrase 'small enough to forget you have it, until you need it.'
legality: Legal — classified as single-use personal safety device; no permit or documentation required; sold over the counter
specifications:
Length: 140mm
Diameter: 18mm
Weight: 45g
Discharge Voltage: 35,000V
Amperage: 0.002A
Charge Capacity: 3 full discharges (single-use, non-rechargeable)
Activation: Squeeze-and-twist (90° rotation of upper third)
Indicator: 3-pip LED charge remaining display
Body: ABS polymer, matte finish
Price: Φ14 per unit / Φ28 two-pack / Φ48 four-pack
tactical_use: The PSR-1 is a contact weapon only — it must be pressed firmly against an attacker to deliver its discharge, and its short length means the user's hand is extremely close to the contact point. It is not a weapon for managing distance or controlling a situation; it is a tool for creating a brief window to disengage from a threat. Self-defense instructors who teach PSR-1 use emphasize that it is a 'run' weapon — you use it to interrupt a threat long enough to create distance and escape, not to incapacitate and detain. Three discharges at 35,000 volts is enough to cause a pain response and momentary disruption in most subjects; it is not enough to reliably incapacitate a determined or augmented attacker.
cultural_context: The PSR-1 is called 'the nudge' in casual speech — a name that understates it slightly, which is part of its social character. It is unglamorous in a way that most weapons are not. There is no street credibility attached to carrying one; it is simply a practical object, like a first-aid patch or a personal alarm, that a significant percentage of GLMZ's adult population carries in a pocket or bag without thinking about it much. In Tier 1 communities, the four-pack is a common gift between friends, family members, or neighbors — a quiet acknowledgment of shared vulnerability that doesn't require conversation.
known_users: general civilian population across all tiers
Tier 1 residents as primary personal defense option
students and young adults in transit-heavy lifestyles
story_hooks: The batch codes on PSR-1 units found at three separate incidents in the same week trace to a vending machine that was serviced by the same technician forty-eight hours before each incident. The technician is missing. The units from that machine all show discharge indicators reading zero — all three charges used — but the forensic evidence at each scene only accounts for one contact event per unit.
